{{Short description|Factors influencing the likelihood of a person having children}}
{{about|determinants that are associated with how many children a person will have in total during their lifetime|determinants of childbearing timing|Advanced maternal age|and|Paternal age effect|the factor in microbiology|Fertility factor (bacteria)}}

'''Fertility factors''' are determinants of the number of children that an individual is likely to have. [[Fertility]] factors are mostly positive or negative [[Correlation does not imply causation|correlations without certain causations]].

Factors associated with increased fertility include the intention to have children,<ref name="balbo2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Balbo N, Billari FC, Mills M | title = Fertility in Advanced Societies: A Review of Research: La fécondité dans les sociétés avancées: un examen des recherches | journal = European Journal of Population | volume = 29 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–38 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 23440941 | pmc = 3576563 | doi = 10.1007/s10680-012-9277-y }}</ref> remaining [[religiosity]],<ref name="HayfordMorgan2008"/> general inter-generational transmission of values,<ref name="balbo2013" /> high status of [[marriage]]<ref name="us2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Martinez G, Daniels K, Chandra A | title = Fertility of men and women aged 15-44 years in the United States: National Survey of Family Growth, 2006-2010 | journal = National Health Statistics Reports | issue = 51 | pages = 1–28 | date = April 2012 | pmid = 22803225 | url = https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr051.pdf | publisher = Division of Vital Statistics, [[National Center for Health Statistics]] | format = primary research report }}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}} and [[cohabitation]],<ref name="fent2013">{{cite journal|year=2013|title=Family policies in the context of low fertility and social structure|journal=Demographic Research|volume=29|issue=37|pages=963–998| last1 = Fent | first1 = Thomas | last2 = Diaz | first2 = Belinda Aparicio | last3 = Prskawetz | first3 = Alexia | author3-link = Alexia Fürnkranz-Prskawetz | name-list-style = vanc |doi=10.4054/DemRes.2013.29.37|doi-access=free|hdl=10419/96953|hdl-access=free}}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}} maternal<ref name="SchaffnitSear2014"/> and social<ref name=balbo2013/> support, rural residence,<ref name="balbo2013" /> a small subset of [[Natalism|pro-family social programs]],<ref name="balbo2013" /> [[fertility and intelligence|low IQ]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shatz |first1=Steven M. | name-list-style = vanc |title=IQ and fertility: A cross-national study |journal=Intelligence |date=March 2008 |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=109–111 |doi=10.1016/j.intell.2007.03.002 }}</ref> personality traits such as [[conscientiousness]], and generally increased food production.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bioinfo.rpi.edu/bystrc/pub/pimentel.pdf|title=Human population numbers as a function of food supply|work=Russel Hopfenburg, David Pimentel, Duke University, Durham, NC, USA;2Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA}}</ref>

Factors generally associated with decreased fertility include rising [[Income and fertility|income]],<ref name="balbo2013" /> value and attitude changes,<ref name="European" /><ref name="balbo2013" /> education,<ref name="balbo2013" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://blogs.worldbank.org/health/female-education-and-childbearing-closer-look-data|title=Female Education and Childbearing: A Closer Look at the Data|last=Pradhan|first=Elina| name-list-style = vanc |date=2015-11-24|website=Investing in Health|language=en|access-date=2019-03-11}}</ref> [[female labor participation]],<ref name=bloom2007/> [[Human population control|population control]],<ref name="Wang Judge"/> age,<ref name="velde2002" /> [[contraception]],<ref name=balbo2013/> partner reluctance to child-bearing,<ref name=balbo2013/> infertility,<ref name="eshre2014" /> [[pollution]],<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2207560-exposure-to-air-pollution-seems-to-negatively-affect-womens-fertility/ |title = Exposure to air pollution seems to negatively affect women's fertility}}</ref> and [[obesity]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Dağ ZÖ, Dilbaz B | title = Impact of obesity on infertility in women | journal = Journal of the Turkish German Gynecological Association | volume = 16 | issue = 2 | pages = 111–7 | date = 1 June 2015 | pmid = 26097395 | pmc = 4456969 | doi = 10.5152/jtgga.2015.15232 }}</ref>

==Factors associated with increased fertility==
=== Intention ===
[[File:Paus family portrait NFB-18645.jpg|thumb|A Norwegian family {{Circa|1900}}, parents plus five children]]
The predictive power of intentions continues to be debated.  Research that argues that intentions are a good predictor of actual results tends to draw ideas from the [[theory of planned behavior]] (TPB).  According to the TPB, intentions stem from three factors: attitudes regarding children, including the cost of raising them versus perceived benefits; subjective norms, for example the influence of others; and perceived control over behavior, that is, how much control an individual has over their own behavior.<ref name="balbo2013" />

Fertility intentions tend to boil down to quantum intentions, or how many children to bear, and tempo intentions, meaning when to have them. Of these, quantum intention is the poor predictor because it tends to change as a result of the ups and downs of a typical life. Tempo intention is a somewhat better predictor, but still a weak way to predict actual results.<ref name="balbo2013" />

The intention to have children generally increases the probability of having children. This relation is well evidenced in advanced societies, where [[birth control]] is the default option.<ref name="balbo2013" />

A comparison of a survey to birth registers in Norway found that parents were more likely to realize their fertility intentions than childless respondents.<ref name="dommermuth2014">{{cite web|url=http://www.ssb.no/en/forskning/discussion-papers/_attachment/182990?_ts=146a3818d38|title=Differences in childbearing by time frame of fertility intention. A study using survey and register data from Norway|year=2014| first1 = Lars | last1 = Dommermuth | first2 = Jane | last2 = Klobas | first3 = Trude | last3 = Lappegård | name-list-style = vanc }} Part of the research project Family Dynamics, Fertility Choices and Family Policy (FAMDYN)</ref> It was also suggested that childless individuals may underestimate the effort of having children.<ref name="dommermuth2014" /> On the other hand, parents may better understand their ability to manage another child.<ref name="dommermuth2014" /> Individuals intending to have children immediately are more likely to achieve this within two years,<ref name="dommermuth2014" /> whereas in contrast, the fertility rate was found to be higher among those intending to have children in the long term (after four years).<ref name="dommermuth2014" /> Stability of fertility intentions further improves the chance to realize them.<ref name="cavalli2013">{{cite journal|year=2013|title=How expected life and partner satisfaction affect women's fertility outcomes: the role of uncertainty in intentions|url=http://muse.jhu.edu/login?auth=0&type=summary&url=/journals/population_review/v052/52.2.cavalli.html|journal=Population Review|volume=52|issue=2| first1 = Laura | last1 = Cavalli | first2 = Jane | last2 = Klobas |doi=10.1353/prv.2013.a523812 | name-list-style = vanc |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Such stability is increased by the belief that having a child will improve [[life satisfaction]] and partner relationships.<ref name="cavalli2013" />

Chances of realizing fertility intentions are lower in [[post-Soviet states]] than in [[Western Europe]]an states.<ref>{{cite journal|year=2014|title=Failure to Realize Fertility Intentions: A Key Aspect of the Post-communist Fertility Transition|journal=Population Research and Policy Review|volume=33|issue=3|pages=393–418|doi=10.1007/s11113-013-9313-6| first1 = Zsolt | last1 = Spéder | first2 = Balázs | last2 = Kapitány |s2cid=154279339| name-list-style = vanc }}</ref>

There are many determinants of the intention to have children, including:
* The ''mother's preference'' of family size, which influences that of the children through early adulthood.<ref name="AxinnClarkberg1994">{{cite journal | vauthors = Axinn WG, Clarkberg ME, Thornton A | title = Family influences on family size preferences | journal = Demography | volume = 31 | issue = 1 | pages = 65–79 | date = February 1994 | pmid = 8005343 | doi = 10.2307/2061908 | jstor = 2061908 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Likewise, the [[extended family]] influences fertility intentions, with an increased number of nephews and nieces increasing the preferred number of children.<ref name="balbo2013" />
* ''Social pressure'' from kin and friends to have another child.<ref name="balbo2013" />
* ''Social support''. A study from [[West Germany]] found that both men receiving no support at all and receiving support from many different people have a lower probability of intending to have another child than those with a moderate degree of support. The negative effect of support from many different people is probably related to coordination problems.<ref name="balbo2013" />
* ''Happiness'', with happier people tending to want more children.<ref name="balbo2013" />
* ''A secure housing situation''.<ref>{{cite journal|year=2013|title=A home to plan the first child? Fertility intentions and housing conditions in Italy|journal=Population, Space and Place|volume=19|pages=60–71|doi=10.1002/psp.1716|last1=Vignoli|first1=Daniele|last2=Rinesi|first2=Francesca|last3=Mussino|first3=Eleonora|name-list-style=vanc|url=http://www.ds.unifi.it/ricerca/pubblicazioni/working_papers/2011/wp2011_04.pdf|access-date=2019-01-01|archive-date=2018-07-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180722042217/http://www.ds.unifi.it/ricerca/pubblicazioni/working_papers/2011/wp2011_04.pdf}}</ref>
* ''Religiosity''.<ref name="Westoff" />

=== Fertility preference ===
The [[Preference theory|Preference Theory]] suggests that a woman's attitudes towards having children are shaped early in life.  Furthermore, these attitudes tend to hold across the life course, and boil down to three main types: career-oriented, family-oriented, and a combination of both work and family. Research shows that family-oriented women have the most children, and work-oriented women have the least, or none at all, although causality remains unclear.<ref name="balbo2013" />

Preferences can also apply to the sex of the children born, and can therefore influence the decisions to have more children.  For instance, if a couple's preference is to have at least one boy and one girl, and the first two children born are boys, there is a significantly high likelihood that the couple will opt to have another child.<ref name="balbo2013" />

===Religiosity===
A survey taken place in 2002 in the United States found that women who reported [[religion]] as "very important" in their everyday lives had a higher fertility than those reporting it as "somewhat important" or "not important".<ref name="HayfordMorgan2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hayford SR, Morgan SP | title = Religiosity and Fertility in the United States: The Role of Fertility Intentions | journal = Social Forces | volume = 86 | issue = 3 | pages = 1163–1188 | year = 2008 | pmid = 19672317 | pmc = 2723861 | doi = 10.1353/sof.0.0000 }}</ref>

For many religions, religiosity is directly associated with an increase in the intention to have children.<ref name="HayfordMorgan2008"/> This appears to be the main means by which religion increases fertility.<ref name=Westoff>{{cite book | title=Third Child: A Study in the Prediction of Fertility| url=https://archive.org/details/thirdchildstudyi0000west| url-access=registration| last1 = Westoff | first1 = Charles F. | last2 = Potter | first2 = R. G. | name-list-style = vanc |location = Princeton, NJ | year=1963| publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-1-4008-7642-6}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=2SDWCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA238 Pages 238-244]</ref> For example, as of 1963, [[Catholic]] couples generally had intentions to have more children than [[Jewish]] couples, who in turn, tended to have more children than [[Protestant]] couples.<ref name=Westoff/> Among Catholics, increased religiosity is associated with the intention to have more children, while on the other hand, increased religiousness among Protestants is associated with the intention to have fewer children.<ref name=Westoff/>

It has also been suggested that religions generally encourage lifestyles with fertility factors that, in turn, increase fertility.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=Agm3KOVeApgC&pg=PA118&lpg=PA118 Page 118] in: {{cite book|title=Male Fertility Patterns and Determinants. Volume 27 of The Springer Series on Demographic Methods and Population Analysis|first = Li | last = Zhang | name-list-style = vanc |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|year=2010|isbn=978-90-481-8939-7}}</ref> For example, [[religious views on birth control]] are, in many religions, more restrictive than secular views, and such religious restrictions have been associated with increased fertility.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schenker JG, Rabenou V | title = Family planning: cultural and religious perspectives | journal = Human Reproduction | volume = 8 | issue = 6 | pages = 969–76 | date = June 1993 | pmid = 8345093 | doi = 10.1093/oxfordjournals.humrep.a138176 }}</ref>

Religion sometimes modifies the fertility effects of education and income. [[Catholic school|Catholic education]] at the university level and the secondary school level was associated in 1963 with higher fertility, even when accounting for the [[confounding]] effect that higher religiosity leads to a higher probability of attending a religiously affiliated school.<ref name=Westoff/> Higher income was also associated with slightly increased fertility among Catholic couples, however, was associated with slightly decreased fertility among Protestant couples.<ref name=Westoff/>

Parents' religiosity is positively associated with their children's fertility. Therefore, more religious parents will tend to increase fertility.<ref name="balbo2013" />

A 2020 study found that the relation between religiosity and fertility was driven by the lower aggregate fertility of secular individuals. While religiosity did not prevent low fertility levels (as some highly religious countries had low fertility rates), secularism did prevent high fertility (as no highly secular country had high fertility rates). Societal level secularism was also a better predictor of religious individuals' fertility than secular individuals, largely due to the effects of cultural values on reproduction, gender and personal autonomy.<ref>Schnabel, Landon. 2016. "Secularism and Fertility Worldwide". SocArXiv. July 19. doi:10.31235/osf.io/pvwpy.</ref>

In the book ''Shall the Religious Inherit the Earth?'', [[Eric Kaufmann]] argues that demographic trends point to religious fundamentalists greatly increasing as a share of the population over the next century.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Shall the religious inherit the earth?|url=https://www.mercatornet.com/articles/view/shall_the_religious_inherit_the_earth/|date=April 6, 2010|website=Mercator Net|access-date=February 27, 2020|archive-date=June 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190623040350/https://www.mercatornet.com/articles/view/shall_the_religious_inherit_the_earth/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=McClendon|first=David|date=Autumn 2013|title=Shall the Religious Inherit the Earth? Demography and Politics in the Twenty-First Century, by ERIC KAUFMANN|url=https://academic.oup.com/socrel/article-abstract/74/3/417/1640161|journal=Sociology of Religion|volume=74|issue=3|pages=417–9|doi=10.1093/socrel/srt026|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Other scholars have argued that this may be a form of "cultural selection" that will affect future demographics due to certain religious groups having high fertility that is unexplained by other factors such as income.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kolk|first1=M.|last2= Cownden |first2=D.|last3=Enquist|first3=M. |title=Correlations in fertility across generations: can low fertility persist?|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences|date=29 January 2014|volume=281|issue=1779|article-number = 20132561 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2013.2561|pmid= 24478294 |pmc=3924067}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Burger|first1=Oskar|last2= DeLong|first2=John P.|title= What if fertility decline is not permanent? The need for an evolutionarily informed approach to understanding low fertility|journal= Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences|date=28 March 2016|volume=371|issue=1692|article-number = 20150157|doi= 10.1098/rstb.2015.0157 |pmid= 27022084|pmc= 4822437}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title= Population paradox: Europe's time bomb |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/europe/population-paradox-europes-time-bomb-888030.html |access-date=31 March 2019 |work=The Independent |date=9 August 2008}}</ref>

===Intergenerational transmission of values===
The transmission of values from parents to offspring ([[Nature versus nurture|nurture]]) has been a core area of fertility research.  The assumption is that parents transmit these [[family values]], preferences, attitudes and religiosity to their children, all of which have long-term effects analogous to genetics.  Researchers have tried to find a causal relationship between, for example, the number of parents' siblings and the number of children born by the parents own children (a quantum effect), or between the age of the first birth of the parents' generation and age of first birth of any of their own children (a tempo effect).<ref name="balbo2013" />

Most studies concerning tempo focus on teenage mothers and show that having had a young mother increases the likelihood of having a child at a young age.<ref name="balbo2013" />

In [[high-income countries]], the number of children a person has strongly correlates with the number of children that each of those children will eventually have.<ref name="Murphy2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Murphy M | title = Cross-national patterns of intergenerational continuities in childbearing in developed countries | journal = Biodemography and Social Biology | volume = 59 | issue = 2 | pages = 101–26 | year = 2013 | pmid = 24215254 | pmc = 4160295 | doi = 10.1080/19485565.2013.833779 }}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}}<ref name="balbo2013" />

Danish data from [[dizygotic twin|non-identical twins]] growing up in the same environment compared to [[identical twin]]s indicated that genetic influences in themselves largely override previously shared environmental influences.<ref name=balbo2013/> The [[birth order]] does not seem to have any effect on fertility.<ref name=Westoff/>

Other studies, however, show that this effect can be balanced by the child's own attitudes that result from personal experiences, religiosity, education, etc. So, although the mother's preference of family size may influence that of the children through early adulthood,<ref name="Murphy2013" /> the child's own attitudes then take over and influence fertility decisions.<ref name="balbo2013" />

===Marriage and cohabitation===
The effect of cohabitation on fertility varies across countries.<ref name="balbo2013" />

In the US cohabitation is generally associated with lower fertility.<ref name="balbo2013" />  However, another study found that cohabiting couples in France have equal fertility as married ones.<ref name=balbo2013/> Russians have also been shown to have a higher fertility within cohabitation.<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Potârcă G, Mills M, Lesnard L |title=Family Formation Trajectories in Romania, the Russian Federation and France: Towards the Second Demographic Transition?|journal=European Journal of Population|year=2013|doi=10.1007/s10680-012-9279-9|volume=29|pages=69–101|s2cid=3270388|url=http://spire.sciencespo.fr/hdl:/2441/53r60a8s3kup1vc9l2o8ij6a6|hdl=11370/7610ea82-0af8-4830-9dd6-e3bbb0da0eed|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Survey data from 2003 in [[Romania]] showed that marriage equalized the [[total fertility rate]] among both highly educated and limited-education people to approximately 1.4. Among those cohabiting, on the other hand, a lower level of education increased the fertility rate to 1.7, and a higher level of education decreased it to 0.7.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Recent Features of Cohabitational and Marital Fertility in Romania | first1 = Jan M. | last1 = Hoem | first2 = Cornelia | last2 = Mureşan | first3 = Mihaela | last3 = Hărăguş | name-list-style = vanc | journal = Population English Edition | year = 2013 | url = http://www.demogr.mpg.de/papers/working/wp-2013-007.pdf | archive-date = 2021-12-01 | access-date = 2016-02-13 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20211201235928/https://www.demogr.mpg.de/papers/working/wp-2013-007.pdf | url-status = dead }}</ref> Another study found that Romanian women with little education have about equal fertility in marital and cohabiting partnerships.<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Hoem | first1 = Jan M. | last2 = Muresan | first2 = Cornelia | name-list-style = vanc |title=The Role of Consensual Unions in Romanian Total Fertility|journal=Stockholm Research Reports in Demography |year=2011 |url= http://www.demogr.mpg.de/en/projects_publications/publications_1904/other_working_papers/the_role_of_consensual_unions_in_romanian_total_fertility_4544.htm |access-date=2016-02-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303104323/http://www.demogr.mpg.de/en/projects_publications/publications_1904/other_working_papers/the_role_of_consensual_unions_in_romanian_total_fertility_4544.htm|archive-date=2016-03-03}}</ref>

A study of the United States, and multiple countries in Europe, found that women who continue to cohabit after giving birth have a significantly lower probability of having a second child than married women in all countries, except those in Eastern Europe.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Perelli-Harris B | title = How Similar are Cohabiting and Married Parents? Second Conception Risks by Union Type in the United States and Across Europe | journal = European Journal of Population | volume = 30 | issue = 4 | pages = 437–464 | year = 2014 | pmid = 25395696 | pmc = 4221046 | doi = 10.1007/s10680-014-9320-2 }}</ref>

===Maternal support===
Data from the [[Generations and Gender Survey]] showed that women with living mothers had earlier first births, while a mother's death early in a daughter's life correlated with a higher probability of childlessness. On the other hand, the survival of fathers had no effect on either outcome. Co-residence with parents delayed first births and resulted in lower total fertility and higher probability of childlessness. This effect is even stronger for poor women.<ref name="SchaffnitSear2014">{{cite journal| vauthors = Schaffnit SB, Sear R |title=Wealth modifies relationships between kin and women's fertility in high-income countries|journal=Behavioral Ecology | volume=25|issue=4|year=2014|pages=834–842|issn=1045-2249|doi=10.1093/beheco/aru059|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Social support===
Social support from the extended family and friends can help a couple decide to have a child, or another one.

Studies mainly in ex-communist Eastern European countries have associated increased fertility with increased [[social capital]] in the form of personal relationships, goods, information, money, work capacity, influence, power, and personal help from others.<ref name="balbo2013" />

Research in the U.S. shows that the extended family willing to provide support becomes a "safety net".  This is particularly important for single mothers and situations involving partnership instability.<ref name="balbo2013" />
[[File:African family poses for a picture in the farm.jpg|thumb|A family of rural Africa]]

===Rural residence===
[[Total fertility rate]]s are higher among women in [[rural area]]s than among women in [[urban area]]s, as evidenced from [[low-income country|low-income]],<ref name=worldbank2015>{{cite book|title=Global Monitoring Report 2015/2016: Development Goals in an Era of Demographic Change|publisher=[[World Bank]] Publications|year=2015|isbn=978-1-4648-0670-4}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=m1z1CgAAQBAJ&pg=PA148 Page 148]</ref> middle-income<ref name=worldbank2015/> and [[high-income countries]].<ref name=balbo2013/> Field researchers have found that fertility rates are high and remain relatively stable among rural populations. Little evidence exists to suggest that high-fertility parents appear to be economically disadvantaged, further strengthening the fact that total fertility rates tend to be higher among women in rural areas.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Caldwell JC | title = The economic rationality of high fertility: An investigation illustrated with Nigerian survey data | journal = Population Studies | volume = 31 | issue = 1 | pages = 5–27 | date = March 1977 | pmid = 22070234 | doi = 10.1080/00324728.1977.10412744 }}</ref> On the other hand, studies have suggested that a higher [[population density]] is associated with decreased fertility rates.<ref name=sato2006>{{citation|url=http://ir.nul.nagoya-u.ac.jp/jspui/bitstream/2237/8650/1/ysatoJUE.pdf|title=Economic geography, fertility and migration|first=Yasuhiro|last=Sato| name-list-style = vanc |journal=Journal of Urban Economics|date=30 July 2006|access-date=31 March 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160206181059/http://ir.nul.nagoya-u.ac.jp/jspui/bitstream/2237/8650/1/ysatoJUE.pdf|archive-date=6 February 2016}}</ref> It is shown through studies that fertility rates differ between regions in ways that reflect the opportunity costs of child rearing. In a region with high population density, women restrain themselves from having many children due to the costs of living, therefore lowering the fertility rates.<ref name="sato2006" /> Within urban areas, people in [[suburb]]s are consistently found to have higher fertility.<ref name=balbo2013/> Some research indicates that population density may explain up to 31% of the variance in fertility rates, although the effect of population density on fertility can be moderated by other factors such as environmental conditions, religiosity and social norms.<ref>Rotella, Amanda, Michael EW Varnum, Oliver Sng, and Igor Grossmann. "Increasing population densities predict decreasing fertility rates over time: A 174-nation investigation." (2020).</ref>

=== Pro-family government programs ===
Many studies have attempted to determine the causal link between government policies and fertility. However, as this article suggests, there are many factors that can potentially affect decisions to have children, how many to have, and when to have them, and separating these factors from effects of a particular government policy is difficult. Making this even more difficult is the time lag between government policy initiation and results.<ref name="balbo2013" />

The purpose of these programs is to reduce the [[opportunity cost]] of having children, either by increasing family income or reducing the cost of children.<ref name="European" />   One study has found a positive effect on number of children during life due to family policy programs that make it easier for women to combine family and employment.  Again, the idea here is to reduce the opportunity cost of children.  These positive results have been found in Germany, Sweden, Canada, and the US.<ref name="pmid20608108">[https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs10680-012-9277-y Balbo 2013] (see top of list), citing: {{cite journal | vauthors = Kalwij A | title = The impact of family policy expenditure on fertility in western Europe | journal = Demography | volume = 47 | issue = 2 | pages = 503–19 | date = May 2010 | pmid = 20608108 | pmc = 3000017 | doi = 10.1353/dem.0.0104 }}</ref>

However, other empirical studies show that these programs are expensive and their impact tends to be small, so currently there is no broad consensus on their effectiveness in raising fertility.<ref name="fent2013" />

===Other factors associated with increased fertility===
Other factors associated with increase of fertility include:
* ''Social pressure'': Women have an increased probability to have another child when there is social pressure from parents, relatives, and friends to do so.<ref name="balbo2013" /> For example, fertility increases during the one to two years after a sibling or a co-worker has a child.<ref name=balbo2013/>
* ''[[Homophily]]:'' an increased [[fertility]] is seen in people with a tendency to seek acquaintance among those with common characteristics.<ref name="fent2013" />
* ''[[Patriarchy]]'': Male-dominated families generally have more children.<ref name="Westoff" />
* ''[[Nuclear family]] households'' have higher fertility than [[Co-living|cooperative living]] arrangements, according to studies both from the [[Western world|Western World]].<ref name=balbo2013/> 
* ''Illegalization of abortion'' temporarily increased birth rates in communist Romania for a few years, but this was followed by a later decline due to an increased use of [[illegal abortion]].<ref name="European" />
* ''[[Assisted reproduction technology]] (ART).'' One study from [[Denmark]] projects an increase in fertility, as a result of ART, that could increase the 1975 birth cohort by 5%.<ref name="balbo2013" /> In addition, ART seems to challenge the biological limits of successful childbearing.<ref name="balbo2013" />
* ''Immigration'' sometimes increases fertility rates of a country because of the births to the immigrant groups.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.prb.org/Publications/Articles/2009/fallingbirthrates.aspx|title=Birth Rates Rising in Some Low Birth-Rate Countries|website=www.prb.org|access-date=2017-03-29|archive-date=2017-03-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170330084905/http://www.prb.org/Publications/Articles/2009/fallingbirthrates.aspx}}</ref> However, over succeeding generations, migrant fertility often converges to that of their new country.<ref name="balbo2013" /> The religiosity factor above, however, provides for various  [[Muslim population growth|systematic exceptions]] to that rule. 

==Factors associated with decreased fertility==
Fertility is declining in advanced societies because couples are having fewer children or none at all, or they are delaying childbirth beyond the woman's most fertile years.  The factors that lead to this trend are complex and probably vary from country to country.<ref name="European" />

===Rising income===
[[File:TFR vs PPP 2015.png|thumb|300px|Graph of [[total fertility rate]] vs. [[List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita|GDP (PPP) per capita of the corresponding country]], 2015<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2127.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070613002952/https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2127.html|archive-date=June 13, 2007|title=Field Listing: Total Fertility Rate|website=[[The World Factbook]]|access-date=2016-04-24}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/resources/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2004rank.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150427163053/https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/resources/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2004rank.html|archive-date=April 27, 2015|title=Country Comparison: GDP - Per Capita (PPP)|website=[[The World Factbook]]|access-date=2016-04-24}}</ref>]]
{{Main|Income and fertility}}
Increased [[gross domestic product|income]] and [[Human Development Index|human development]] are generally associated with decreased fertility rates.<ref name=rai2013/> Economic theories about declining fertility postulate that people earning more have a higher [[opportunity cost]] if they focus on childbirth and parenting rather than continuing their careers,<ref name=balbo2013/> that women who can economically sustain themselves have less incentive to become married,<ref name=balbo2013/> and that higher income parents value quality over quantity and so spend their resources on fewer children.<ref name="balbo2013" />

On the other hand, there is some evidence that with rising economic development, fertility rates drop at first, but then begin to rise again as the level of social and economic development increases, while still remaining below the [[replacement rate]].<ref>{{cite news|title=The best of all possible worlds? A link between wealth and breeding|url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2009/08/06/the-best-of-all-possible-worlds|newspaper=The Economist|date=August 6, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Myrskylä M, Kohler HP, Billari FC | title = Advances in development reverse fertility declines | journal = Nature | volume = 460 | issue = 7256 | pages = 741–3 | date = August 2009 | pmid = 19661915 | doi = 10.1038/nature08230 | bibcode = 2009Natur.460..741M | s2cid = 4381880 }}</ref>

=== Value and attitude changes ===
While some researchers cite economic factors as the main driver of fertility decline, socio-cultural theories focus on changes in values and attitudes toward children as being primarily responsible.  For example, the [[Demographic transition|Second Demographic Transition]] reflects changes in personal goals, religious preferences, relationships, and perhaps most important, family formations.<ref name="European" /> Also, [[Preference Theory]] attempts to explain how women's choices regarding work versus family have changed and how the expansion of options and the freedom to choose the option that seems best for them are the keys to recent declines in [[Total fertility rate|TFR]].<ref name="European" />

A comparative study in Europe found that family-oriented women had the most children, work-oriented women had fewer or no children, and that among other factors, preferences play a major role in deciding to remain childless.<ref name="balbo2013" />

Another example of this can be found in Europe and in [[post-Soviet states]], where values of increased autonomy and independence have been associated with decreased fertility.<ref name="balbo2013" />

===Education===
Results from research which attempts to find causality between education and fertility is mixed.<ref name="balbo2013" /> One theory holds that higher educated women are more likely to become career women. Also, for higher educated women, there is a higher opportunity cost to bearing children. Both would lead higher educated women to postpone marriage and births.<ref name="balbo2013" /> However, other studies suggest that, although higher educated women may postpone marriage and births, they can recuperate at a later age so that the impact of higher education is negligible.<ref name="balbo2013" />

In the [[United States]], a large survey found that women with a bachelor's degree or higher had an average of 1.1 children, while those with no high school diploma or equivalent had an average of 2.5 children.<ref name=us2012/> For men with the same levels of education, the number of children was 1.0 and 1.7, respectively.<ref name=us2012/>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}}

In [[Europe]], on the other hand, women who are more educated eventually have about as many children as do the less educated, but that education results in having children at an older age.<ref name=balbo2013/> Likewise, a study in [[Norway]] found that better-educated males have a decreased probability of remaining childless, although they generally became fathers at an older age.<ref name="KravdalRindfuss2008">{{cite journal|vauthors=Rindfuss RR, Kravdal O|year=2008|title=Changing Relationships between Education and Fertility: A Study of Women and Men Born 1940 to 1964|journal=American Sociological Review|volume=73|issue=5|pages=854–873|doi=10.1177/000312240807300508|issn=0003-1224|hdl=10419/63098|s2cid=56286073|url=http://www.sv.uio.no/econ/english/research/unpublished-works/working-papers/pdf-files/2007/Memo-11-2007.pdf|archive-date=2017-08-08|access-date=2019-09-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808133730/http://www.sv.uio.no/econ/english/research/unpublished-works/working-papers/pdf-files/2007/Memo-11-2007.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[Catholic school|Catholic education]] at the university level and, to a lesser degree, at the secondary school level, was associated with higher fertility, even when accounting for the confounding effect that higher religiosity among Catholics leads to a higher probability of attending a religiously affiliated school.<ref name=Westoff/>

The level of a country's development often determines the level of women's education required to affect fertility.  Countries with lower levels of development and gender equivalence are likely to find that a higher level of women's education, greater than secondary level, is required to affect fertility. Studies suggest that in many sub-Saharan African countries fertility decline is linked to female education.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kebede E, Goujon A, Lutz W | title = Stalls in Africa's fertility decline partly result from disruptions in female education | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 116 | issue = 8 | pages = 2891–2896 | date = February 2019 | pmid = 30718411 | pmc = 6386713 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1717288116 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2019PNAS..116.2891K }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://blogs.worldbank.org/health/female-education-and-childbearing-closer-look-data|title=Female Education and Childbearing: A Closer Look at the Data|last=Pradhan|first=Elina| name-list-style = vanc |date=2015-11-24|website=Investing in Health|language=en|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> Having said this, fertility in undeveloped countries can still be significantly reduced in the absence of any improvement in the general level of formal education. For example, During the period 1997-2002 (15 years), fertility in Bangladesh fell by almost 40%, despite the fact that literacy rates (especially those of women) did not increase significantly. This reduction has been attributed to that country's family planning program, which could be called a form of [[informal education]].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal| first = Wardatul | last = Akmam | name-list-style = vanc |year=2002|title=Women's Education and Fertility Rates in Developing Countries, With Special Reference to Bangladesh|url=http://www.eubios.info/EJ124/ej124i.htm|journal=Eubios Journal of Asian and International Bioethics|volume=12|pages=138–143}}</ref>

===Population control===

{{Further|Human population control}}
During the second part of the 20th century, several countries, especially in [[Asia]], have implemented official or unofficial population policies meant to decrease family size, such as [[one-child policy]] or [[two child policy]]. [[China]] and [[India]] have the oldest and the largest [[human population control]] programs in the world.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9781137319494_3 |chapter=Global Population and Demographic Trends |title=New Age Globalization |year=2013 |last1=Ahmad |first1=Aqueil| name-list-style = vanc |pages=33–60 |isbn=978-1-349-45115-9 }}</ref> In China, a [[one-child policy]] was introduced between 1978 and 1980,<ref name="adc">{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhu WX | title = The one child family policy | journal = Archives of Disease in Childhood | volume = 88 | issue = 6 | pages = 463–4 | date = June 2003 | pmid = 12765905 | pmc = 1763112 | doi = 10.1136/adc.88.6.463 }}</ref> and began to be formally phased out in 2015 in favor of a [[two-child policy]].<ref name="HeskethZhou2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hesketh T, Zhou X, Wang Y | title = The End of the One-Child Policy: Lasting Implications for China | journal = JAMA | volume = 314 | issue = 24 | pages = 2619–20 | year = 2015 | pmid = 26545258 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2015.16279 }}</ref> The total fertility rate in China fell from 2.8 births per woman in 1979 to 1.5 in 2010.<ref name="Wang Judge">{{cite journal|first1= Wang|last1= Feng|last2= Yong|first2= Cai|first3= Baochang|last3= Gu|name-list-style= vanc|title= Population, Policy, and Politics: How Will History Judge China's One-Child Policy?|journal= Population and Development Review|volume= 38|date= 2012|pages= 115–29|doi= 10.1111/j.1728-4457.2013.00555.x|doi-access= free}}</ref> However, the efficacy of the one-child policy itself is not clear, since there was already a sharp reduction from more than five births per woman in the early 1970s, before the introduction of the one-child policy.<ref name="Wang Judge"/> It has thereby been suggested that a decline in fertility rate would have continued even without the strict [[antinatalist]] policy.<ref>{{cite book|title=World Population: A Reference Handbook (Contemporary world issues)| first = Geoffrey | last = Gilbert | name-list-style = vanc |publisher=ABC-CLIO|year=2005|isbn=978-1-85109-927-6}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=sNSRkLVemxoC&pg=PA25 Page 25]</ref> In 2015 China ended its one child policy, allowing couples to have two children. This was a result of China having a large [[dependency ratio]] with its ageing population and working force.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-34665539|title=China to end one-child policy and allow two | date=29 October 2015|work=BBC News}}</ref> In May 2021, the [[general secretaryship of Xi Jinping]] formally introduced the [[three-child policy]] to replace the two-child policy.<ref name=":5" /> 

[[Vietnam]] has had a population policy for over 60 years. It was launched by the [[Vietnamese government]] in the early 1960s in [[North Vietnam]] and continued in a modified form throughout all of Vietnam (not just the north),<ref name="Princeton Population">{{cite web |last1=Pham |first1=Bang Nguyen |last2=Hill |first2=Peter S |last3=Hall |first3=Wayne |last4=Rao |first4=Chalapati |title=The Evolution of Population Policy in Viet Nam |url=http://epc2012.princeton.edu/papers/120007 |publisher=School of Population Health, University of Queensland |access-date=12 March 2015}}</ref> until 2025, when due to a [[sub-replacement fertility]] rate, the communist government lifted all regulations regarding the number of children families are allowed to have.<ref>https://english.news.cn/asiapacific/20250604/9b625ab09f844a17a9f65da7f0dc6b9e/c.html</ref> The two-child policy, in force until 2025, emphasized the official family-size goal to be ''một hoặc hai con,'' which means "one or two children."<ref name="Population Council Daniel Goodkind">{{cite journal |last1=Goodkind |first1=Daniel |title=Vietnam's One-or-Two-Child Policy in Action |journal=Population and Development Review |date=March 1995 |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=85–111 |jstor=2137414|doi=10.2307/2137414}}</ref>

In the 1970s, in [[British Hong Kong]], families were urged to have maximum two children, although this was not mandated by law, and was instead part of the family planning campaign "Two is Enough".<ref>https://web.archive.org/web/20090327235233/http://www.famplan.org.hk/fpahk/en/template1.asp?style=template1.asp&content=about%2Fhistory.asp</ref>

In [[South Korea]], following the surge in births after the [[Korean War]], the government, starting in 1961, developed population policies meant to suppress population growth, which continued to be implemented in the 1970s and 1980s.<ref>https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9623034/</ref> In 1983, for the first time, the TFR dropped to 2.06, below the replacement rate of 2.1.<ref>https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9623034/</ref>

In the 1990s, in [[Iran]], the government stated that Islam favoured families with two children, as part of its population policy.<ref>Abrahamian, ''History of Modern Iran'', (2008), p.184</ref> 

Extensive efforts have been put into [[family planning in India]]. The fertility rate has dropped from 5.7 in 1966 to 2.4 in 2016.<ref name="ramu2006">{{Citation | title=Brothers and sisters in India: a study of urban adult siblings | vauthors = Ramu GN | publisher=University of Toronto Press | isbn=978-0-8020-9077-5 | year=2006 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2cGSay9VxsgC}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/india/ |title=CIA, The World Fact Book, India, 7/24/2017 |date=10 August 2022 |access-date=24 January 2021 |archive-date=18 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210318202107/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/india |url-status=dead }}</ref> Still,  by 2010, India's family planning program was regarded as only partially successful in controlling fertility rates.<ref>{{cite book|title=Better India, A Better World | last = Murthy | first = N.R.Narayana | name-list-style = vanc |publisher=Penguin Books India |year=2010| isbn=978-0-14-306857-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E5FfYJmodk0C&pg=PA98| page=98}}</ref> By 2023, India's TFR declined to 1.9, although the TFR varies by [[States and union territories of India|state]].<ref>https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/rural-indias-total-fertility-rate-dips-to-replacement-rate/articleshow/123706269.cms</ref>

===Female labor force participation===
Increased participation of [[women in the workforce]] is associated with decreased fertility. A multi-country [[panel study]] found this effect to be strongest among women aged 20–39, with a less strong but persistent effect among older women as well.<ref name=bloom2007>{{cite journal |first1=David |last1=Bloom |first2=David |last2=Canning |first3=Günther |last3=Fink |first4=Jocelyn |last4=Finlay | name-list-style = vanc |year=2009 |title=Fertility, female labor force participation, and the demographic dividend |journal=[[Journal of Economic Growth]] |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=79–101 |doi=10.1007/s10887-009-9039-9 |doi-access=free }}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}}{{better source needed|date=April 2016}} International [[United Nations]] data suggests that women who work because of economic necessity have higher fertility than those who work because they want to do so.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.un.org/esa/population/publications/completingfertility/RevisedLIMpaper.PDF|title=Female Labour-Force Participation| first = Lin Lean | last = Lim | name-list-style = vanc |publisher=[[United Nations]]}}, part of {{cite book|title=Completing the Fertility Transition|year=2009|publisher=[[United Nations]] Publications|isbn=978-92-1-151370-7}}</ref>

However, for countries in the [[Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development|OECD]] area, increased female labor participation has been associated with increased fertility.<ref>{{cite journal |title=A Note on the Changing Relationship between Fertility and Female Employment Rates in Developed Countries| first1 = Namkee | last1 = Ahn | first2 = Pedro | last2 = Mira | name-list-style = vanc |journal=Journal of Population Economics |volume=15 |issue=4 |year=2002 |pages=667–682 |jstor=20007839 |doi=10.1007/s001480100078 | hdl = 10902/25166 | s2cid = 17755082 |url=http://documentos.fedea.net/pubs/eee/eee13.pdf }}</ref>

Causality analyses indicate that fertility rate influences female labor participation, not the other way around.<ref name=balbo2013/>

Women who work in nurturing professions such as teaching and health generally have children at an earlier age.<ref name=balbo2013/> It is theorized that women often self-select themselves into jobs with a favorable [[work–life balance]] in order to pursue both motherhood and employment.<ref name=balbo2013/>

===Pensions===
Some [[pension]] systems can decrease the incentive to have children,<ref name=balbo2013/><ref name="i580">{{cite journal | last1=Danzer | first1=Alexander M. | last2=Zyska | first2=Lennard | title=Pensions and Fertility: Microeconomic Evidence | journal=American Economic Journal: Economic Policy | volume=15 | issue=2 | date=2023-05-01 | issn=1945-7731 | doi=10.1257/pol.20200440 | pages=126–165 | url=https://pubs.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/pol.20200440 | access-date=2026-02-09| url-access=subscription }}</ref> in effect insuring individuals against [[voluntary childlessness]].<ref name="b645">{{cite journal | last=Sinn | first=Hans-Werner | title=The pay-as-you-go pension system as fertility insurance and an enforcement device | journal=Journal of Public Economics | volume=88 | issue=7-8 | date=2004 | doi=10.1016/S0047-2727(03)00015-X | pages=1335–1357 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S004727270300015X | access-date=2026-02-09| url-access=subscription }}</ref> In countries without pensions children can form an [[Old-age-security hypothesis|old-age-security]].

===Age===
{{Main|Advanced maternal age|Paternal age effect}}
[[File:Age and female fertility.svg|thumb|300px|Cumulative percentage and average age for women reaching [[subfertility]], [[Infertility|sterility]], [[irregular menstruation]] and [[menopause]]<ref name=velde2002>{{cite journal | vauthors = te Velde ER, Pearson PL | title = The variability of female reproductive ageing | journal = Human Reproduction Update | volume = 8 | issue = 2 | pages = 141–54 | year = 2002 | pmid = 12099629 | doi = 10.1093/humupd/8.2.141 | doi-access = free }}</ref>]]
Regarding [[age and female fertility]], fertility starts at [[menarche|onset of menses]], typically around age 12-13<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Anderson SE, Dallal GE, Must A | title = Relative weight and race influence average age at menarche: results from two nationally representative surveys of US girls studied 25 years apart | journal = Pediatrics | volume = 111 | issue = 4 Pt 1 | pages = 844–50 | date = April 2003 | pmid = 12671122 | doi = 10.1542/peds.111.4.844 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Al-Sahab B, Ardern CI, Hamadeh MJ, Tamim H | title = Age at menarche in Canada: results from the National Longitudinal Survey of Children & Youth | journal = BMC Public Health | volume = 10 | article-number = 736 | date = November 2010 | pmid = 21110899 | pmc = 3001737 | doi = 10.1186/1471-2458-10-736 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://vstudentworld.yolasite.com/resources/final_yr/gynae_obs/Hamilton%20Fairley%20Obstetrics%20and%20Gynaecology%20Lecture%20Notes%202%20Ed.pdf |title=Obstetrics and Gynaecology: Lecture Notes |edition=2nd |last=Hamilton-Fairley |first=Diana |publisher=Blackwell Publishing |year=2004 |access-date=2012-08-26 |archive-date=2018-10-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181009065351/http://vstudentworld.yolasite.com/resources/final_yr/gynae_obs/Hamilton%20Fairley%20Obstetrics%20and%20Gynaecology%20Lecture%20Notes%202%20Ed.pdf }}</ref> Most women become [[subfertility|subfertile]] during the early 30s, and during the early 40s most women become [[infertility|sterile]].<ref name=velde2002/>

Regarding [[paternal age effect|age and male fertility]], men have decreased pregnancy rates, increased time to pregnancy, and increased infertility as they age, although the correlation is not as substantial as in women.<ref name="Kidd-2001">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kidd SA, Eskenazi B, Wyrobek AJ | title = Effects of male age on semen quality and fertility: a review of the literature | journal = Fertility and Sterility | volume = 75 | issue = 2 | pages = 237–48 | date = February 2001 | pmid = 11172821 | doi = 10.1016/S0015-0282(00)01679-4 | doi-access = free }}</ref> When [[Controlling for a variable|controlling for]] the age of the female partner, comparisons between men under 30 and men over 50 found relative decreases in pregnancy rates between 23% and 38%.<ref name="Kidd-2001"/>

An Indian study found that couples where the woman is less than one year younger than the man have a total mean
number of children of 3.1, compared to 3.5 when the woman is 7–9 years younger than the man.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Influence of age gap between couples on contraception and fertility |vauthors=Das KC, Gautam V, Das K, Tripathy PK |journal=Journal of Family Welfare |url=http://medind.nic.in/jah/t11/i2/jaht11i2p30.pdf |volume=57 |issue=2 |year=2011 |access-date=2016-02-20 |archive-date=2019-08-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190819062932/http://medind.nic.in/jah/t11/i2/jaht11i2p30.pdf }}</ref>

===Contraception===
The "contraceptive revolution" has played a crucial role in reducing the number of children (quantum) and postponing child-bearing (tempo).<ref name="balbo2013" />

Periods of decreased use of [[contraceptive pill]]s due to fears of side effects have been linked with increased fertility in the United Kingdom.<ref name="balbo2013" /> Introductions of laws that increase access to contraceptives have been associated with decreased fertility in the United States.<ref name="balbo2013" /> However, short-term decreases in fertility may reflect a [[Sub-replacement fertility#Tempo effect|tempo effect]] of later childbearing, with individuals using contraceptives catching up later in life. A review of long-term fertility in Europe did not find fertility rates to be directly affected by availability of contraceptives.<ref name="European">{{cite journal | author = The ESHRE Capri Workshop Group | title = Europe the continent with the lowest fertility | journal = Human Reproduction Update | volume = 16 | issue = 6 | pages = 590–602 | year = 2010 | pmid = 20603286 | doi = 10.1093/humupd/dmq023 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

=== Partner and partnership ===
The decision to bear a child in advanced societies generally requires agreement between both partners.  Disagreement between partners may mean that the desire for children of one partner are not realized.<ref name="balbo2013" />

The last several decades have also seen changes in partnership dynamics.  This has led to a tendency toward later marriages and a rise in unmarried cohabitation. Both of these have been linked to the postponement of parenthood (tempo) and thus reduced fertility.<ref name="balbo2013" />

=== Infertility ===
{{Further|Infertility}}
20-30% percent of infertility cases are due to [[male infertility]], 20–35% are due to [[female infertility]], and 25-40% are due to combined problems.<ref name=eshre2014>{{cite web|url=https://www.eshre.eu/guidelines-and-legal/art-fact-sheet.aspx|title=ART fact sheet (July 2014)|website=[[European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304060954/https://www.eshre.eu/Guidelines-and-Legal/ART-fact-sheet.aspx|archive-date=2016-03-04}}</ref> In 10–20% of cases, no cause is found.<ref name=eshre2014/>

The most common cause of [[female infertility]] is ovulatory problems, which generally manifest themselves by sparse or absent menstrual periods.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nhs.uk/Conditions/Infertility/Pages/causes.aspx|title=Causes of infertility|website=[[National Health Service]]|access-date=2018-11-17|date=2017-10-23|archive-date=2016-02-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160229143114/http://www.nhs.uk/Conditions/Infertility/Pages/Causes.aspx}}</ref> [[Male infertility]] is most commonly caused by deficiencies in the [[semen]]: [[semen quality]] is used as a surrogate measure of male fecundity.<ref name=who2010>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cooper TG, Noonan E, von Eckardstein S, Auger J, Baker HW, Behre HM, Haugen TB, Kruger T, Wang C, Mbizvo MT, Vogelsong KM | display-authors = 6 | title = World Health Organization reference values for human semen characteristics | journal = Human Reproduction Update | volume = 16 | issue = 3 | pages = 231–45 | year = 2009 | pmid = 19934213 | doi = 10.1093/humupd/dmp048 | doi-access =  }}</ref>

===Other factors associated with decreased fertility===
* ''Intense relationships''. A Dutch study found that couples are likely to have fewer children if they have high levels of either negative or positive interaction.<ref name="RijkenLiefbroer2008">{{cite journal|last1=Rijken|first1=Arieke J.|last2=Liefbroer|first2=Aart C. | name-list-style = vanc |title=The Influence of Partner Relationship Quality on Fertility [L'influence de la qualité de la relation avec le partenaire sur la fécondité] | journal=European Journal of Population / Revue Européenne de Démographie | volume=25 | issue=1 | year=2008 | pages=27–44 | issn=0168-6577 | doi=10.1007/s10680-008-9156-8 | doi-access=free | hdl=11370/2a4e84da-7576-4189-81cb-516261fdb585 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}}
* ''Unstable relationships'', according to a [[systematic review|review]] in Europe.<ref name=European/>
* ''Higher tax rates''.<ref name="balbo2013" />
* ''Unemployment''. A study in the USA shows that unemployment in women has effects both in the short and the long term in reducing their fertility rate.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Currie J, Schwandt H | title = Short- and long-term effects of unemployment on fertility | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 111 | issue = 41 | pages = 14734–9 | date = October 2014 | pmid = 25267622 | pmc = 4205620 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1408975111 | bibcode = 2014PNAS..11114734C | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* ''Hot weather'' is suggested as a factor in some research.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barreca |first1=Alan |last2=Deschenes |first2=Olivier |last3=Guldi |first3=Melanie |date=2018 |title=Maybe Next Month? Temperature Shocks and Dynamic Adjustments in Birth Rates |journal=Demography |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=1269–1293 |doi=10.1007/s13524-018-0690-7 |issn=0070-3370 |pmc=7457515 |pmid=29968058}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tulane University, USA |last2=Barreca |first2=Alan |date=2017 |title=Does hot weather affect human fertility? |url=https://wol.iza.org/articles/does-hot-weather-affect-human-fertility |journal=[[IZA World of Labor]] |doi=10.15185/izawol.375|doi-access=free }}</ref>
==More complex factors==

=== Delayed childbearing and tempo effect ===
{{see also|Tempo effect}}
The trend of couples forming partnerships and marrying at later ages has been going on for some time. For example, in the US, during the period 1970 to 2006, the average age of first-time mothers increased by 3.6 years, from 21.4 years to 25.0 years.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Mathews TJ |date=August 2009|title=Delayed Childbearing: More Women Are Having Their First Child Later in Life|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/databriefs/db21.pdf|journal=NCHS Data Brief|volume=21|page=1}}</ref>

Also, fertility postponement has become common in all European countries, including those of the former Soviet Union.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Freja|first=Tomas| name-list-style = vanc |date=July 2008|title=Fertility in Europe: Diverse, delayed and below replacement|url=https://www.demographic-research.org/volumes/vol19/3/19-3.pdf|journal=Demographic Research|volume= 19, Article 3|page=20}}</ref>

Nevertheless, delayed childbirth alone is not sufficient to reduce fertility rates: in France despite the average high age at first birth, fertility rate remains close to the 2.1 replacement value.<ref name="European" />  The aggregate effects of delayed childbearing tend to be relatively minor, because most women still have their first child well before the onset of infertility.<ref name=":1" />

===Additional variables===
The following have been reported, at least in the primary research literature, to have no or uncertain effects.
* ''Government support of [[assisted reproductive technology]] (ART)'' like IVF, whereas policies that transfer cash to families for pregnancy, and child support have only a limited effect on total fertility rate, according to the same review.<ref name=European/>
* ''Relationship quality and stability'' have complex relations to fertility, wherein couples with a medium-quality relationship appear to be the most likely to have another child.<ref name=balbo2013/>
* ''Governmental maternity leave benefits'' have no significant effect on fertility, according to one primary source.<ref name="gauthier1997">{{cite journal|vauthors = Gauthier A, Hatzius J |year=1997 |title=Family benefits and fertility: An econometric analysis |journal=Population Studies |volume=51 |issue=3 |jstor=2952473 |doi=10.1080/0032472031000150066 |pages=295–306}}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}}
* ''Children from previous unions''. A study in the United Kingdom found that partners with children from previous unions have a higher likelihood of having children together.<ref name=balbo2013/> A study in France found the opposite, that childbearing rates are lowest after re-partnering if both partners are already parents.<ref name=Beaujouan>{{cite journal| vauthors = Beaujouan E |title=Second-Union Fertility in France: Partners' Age and Other Factors|journal=Population English Edition|volume=66|issue=2|page=239|year=2011|url=http://www.cairn-int.info/article-E_POPU_1102_0275--second-union-fertility-in-france-partner.htm|doi=10.3917/pope.1102.0239|s2cid=145016461}}</ref> The French study also found that in couples where only one was already a parent, fertility rates were about the same as in childless couples.<ref name=Beaujouan/>
* ''Spousal height difference''.<ref name="KrzyżanowskaMascie-Taylor2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Krzyżanowska M, Mascie-Taylor CG, Thalabard JC | title = Is human mating for height associated with fertility? Results from a British National Cohort Study | journal = American Journal of Human Biology | volume = 27 | issue = 4 | pages = 553–63 | year = 2015 | pmid = 25645540 | doi = 10.1002/ajhb.22684 | s2cid = 38106234 }}</ref> Could be explained by all manner of visible [[Sexual dimorphism|sexual dimorphisms]] priming for other instinctual functions associated with reproduction.  
* ''Mother's health'' is also a great determinant of the state of health of the unborn child, mother's death in childbirth means almost certain death for her newly born child.<ref name="prb.org">{{Cite web|url=http://www.prb.org/Publications/Reports/2002/HealthyMothersandHealthyNewbornsTheVitalLink.aspx|title=Healthy Mothers and Healthy Newborns: The Vital Link|website=www.prb.org|access-date=2017-03-29|archive-date=2017-03-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170330084244/http://www.prb.org/Publications/Reports/2002/HealthyMothersandHealthyNewbornsTheVitalLink.aspx}}</ref>
* ''Birth spacing'' refers to the timing and frequency of pregnancies. Childbirth to a mother is affected by this factor in one way or the other.<ref name="prb.org"/>
* ''Familism.'' The fertility impact is unknown in country-level [[familism]] systems, where the majority of the economic and caring responsibilities rest on the family (such as in Southern Europe), as opposed to defamilialized systems, where welfare and caring responsibilities are largely supported by the state (such as Nordic countries).<ref name="balbo2013" />

==Racial and ethnic factors==
{{update|section|date=August 2024}}
In the [[United States]], [[Hispanic]]s, and [[African American]]s have earlier and higher fertility than other racial and ethnic groups. In 2009, the teen birth rate for Hispanics between the age 15-19 was roughly 80 births per 1000 women. The teen birth rate for African Americans in 2009 was 60 births per 1000 women and 20 for non Hispanic teens (white).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kearney MS, Levine PB | title = Why is the teen birth rate in the United States so high and why does it matter? | journal = The Journal of Economic Perspectives | volume = 26 | issue = 2 | pages = 141–66 | date = 2012-01-01 | pmid = 22792555 | doi = 10.1257/jep.26.2.141 | doi-access = free | jstor = 41495308 }}</ref>  According to the United States census, State Health Serve and the CDC, Hispanics accounted for 23% of the birth in 2014 out of the 1,000,000 births in the United States.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=January 2016|title=American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology|journal=Birth Rates Among Hispanics and Non-Hispanics and Their Representation in Clinical Trials in Obstetrics and Gynecology|volume=214|pages=S296–S297|doi=10.1016/j.ajog.2015.10.595 | last1 = Kahr | first1 = Maike K | name-list-style = vanc |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=us2012/>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}}

==Multifactorial analyses==
{{more science citations needed | section|date=April 2016}}
A [[regression analysis]] on a population in India resulted in the following equation of [[total fertility rate]], where parameters preceded by a plus were associated with increased fertility, and parameters preceded by a minus were associated with decreased fertility:<ref name=rai2013>{{cite journal | vauthors=Rai PK, Pareek S, Joshi H | title=Regression Analysis of Collinear Data using r-k Class Estimator: Socio-Economic and Demographic Factors Affecting the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) in India | journal=Journal of Data Science | format=primary research article | year=2013 | volume=11 | issue=2 | pages=323–342 | doi=10.6339/JDS.2013.11(2).1030 | s2cid=59042059 | url=http://www.jds-online.com/file_download/394/JDS-1130.pdf | access-date=12 April 2016 | archive-date=25 November 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191125111417/http://www.jds-online.com/file_download/394/JDS-1130.pdf }}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=April 2016}}

Total Fertility Rate = 0.02 ([[human&nbsp;development&nbsp;index]]*) +&nbsp;0.07 ([[infant&nbsp;mortality&nbsp;rate]]*) −&nbsp;0.34 ([[contraceptive]]&nbsp;use) +&nbsp;0.03 (male&nbsp;age&nbsp;at&nbsp;marriage*) −&nbsp;0.21 (female&nbsp;age&nbsp;at&nbsp;marriage) −&nbsp;0.16 (birth&nbsp;interval) −&nbsp;0.26 (use&nbsp;of&nbsp;improved&nbsp;[[water&nbsp;quality]]) +&nbsp;0.03 (male&nbsp;literacy&nbsp;rate*) −&nbsp;0.01 (female&nbsp;literacy rate*) −&nbsp;0.30 ([[Midwifery|maternal&nbsp;care]])

<nowiki>*</nowiki> = Parameter did not reach [[statistical significance]] on its own
